chapter: Corrections and views on early Black music
title: Disputing Duke Ellington's claim about Black reading musicians
summary: White disputes that there were no reading Black pianists before 1915, citing Tony Jackson, Michael, Murray and Smalls's father in Charleston.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: He was reading every doc you put before him, early than 1900 even. As early as 1900, as a little boy, he was schooled in his place.
He was studying music in 1900. Or he wouldn't be considered one of the best teachers down there.

Papa, I'm afraid of all of them, give him that credit. Go to Emanuel Moneta, he'll school you on the piano. He'll teach you your proper fingers. And if he wants to sit there and maybe age has got him a little bit down, but he knows all his, he's going to give you the proper execution for fingers. He can get around. See, what Duke Ellington put in his book there were no reading. What are you going to do with Tony Jackson? My God Almighty. What are you going to do with Michael, who's older than these fellas? Oh yeah. You see, Michael read every doc you put before him.

What are you going to do about Murray down there in Jacksonville, Florida? All those fellas who read. You see, Dr. Locke wrote a book like that too. Oh yeah, I've read that. Yeah, and I could kick him all in the pants around some place for writing that kind of thing about there were no Negro musicians, no Negro bands of consequences. He didn't know. No. So he ought to devote himself to his time to the subject he teaches in Howard and leave this part up to somebody who knows. He was a little bit of a piece of advice for Duke Ellington, he didn't come on the scene until 1927. And I happened to be in New York when he was playing with five pieces for the man whom I went to school with at Avery Normal Institute. Smalls.

And Smalls's father was one of the finest pianists organ teachers in Charleston, South Carolina. Professor Duncan, Professor Smalls, and Professor Foster, they all talked down there. And you had to read your music. So he should be ashamed to write those things unless he gets some factules about it. Who ever heard about Duke Ellington before 1900 to say any how 40? Yeah.
It was never, of course he made it all hit at the Cockney Club in 1932. That's right.
